title: Unlabeled UTF-8 documents with <!DOCTYPE html> are still decoded with the legacy locale fallback (e.g. EUC-KR on Korean systems)

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body:
### What is the issue with the HTML Standard? The encoding sniffing algorithm still ends with an "implementation-defined or user-specified default", and the spec's suggested defaults table maps locales to legacy encodings (e.g. `ko` → EUC-KR, `en` → windows-1252). Browsers also deliberately exclude UTF-8 from content-based detection for http(s) URLs (it is only a possible outcome for `file:` URLs). In practice this keeps biting today's authors, because the most common way a modern UTF-8 page ends up unlabeled is not legacy content but a local or ad-hoc static server that sends `Content-Type: text/html` with no `charset` (Python's `http.server`, many dev servers, quick tunnels, object storage), combined with a page that forgot ``. **Reproduction** (Chrome stable on Windows, Korean UI locale): ```html repro

남은 공간 54GB - 누가 쓰고 있을까요?

``` Saved as UTF-8 with no BOM, served with `python3 -m http.server` (`Content-Type: text/html`, no charset) over https, it renders as: ``` �궓��� 怨듦컙 54GB - �늻媛� �벐怨� �엳�쓣源뚯슂? ``` The bytes are valid UTF-8 throughout, and the document has the HTML5 doctype, so it cannot be a pre-UTF-8 legacy page. Yet the user sees mojibake, and the result depends on the reader's OS locale (an `en` user gets windows-1252 mojibake instead). ### Prior discussion I am aware this has been discussed and rejected before. The main reasons I found were: 1. Unlabeled legacy content would break if the fallback became UTF-8. 2. A UTF-8 fallback would encourage more unlabeled content. 3. Content arrives incrementally: when the first bytes are ASCII-only, the decision has to be made before non-ASCII appears. Related: W3C Bug 15076 (UTF-8 fallback when the HTML5 doctype is present, 2011), the "Default encoding to UTF-8?" whatwg thread (Dec 2011), whatwg/encoding#68, and https://hsivonen.fi/utf-8-detection/. ### Why revisit now - Unlabeled *legacy* content is a shrinking, mostly static corpus. Firefox telemetry from Firefox 86 already found unlabeled UTF-8 more common than unlabeled legacy encodings. - Reason 2 has not held up. Authors who hit this do not learn to label their pages. They learn that "Korean text breaks in Chrome on some machines", and every reader on a different locale sees something different. The current behaviour does not teach anyone. It only makes the same bytes render differently per locale. - Both Gecko (chardetng) and Chromium (CED) already run a content-based detector on unlabeled documents and already know when the input is valid UTF-8. Only the policy excludes UTF-8 as an outcome. ### Possible narrower changes (any one would help) 1. **Doctype-gated UTF-8 outcome.** If the document starts with `` and has no BOM, no transport-layer charset and no ``, allow the detector to return UTF-8 when the bytes seen so far are valid UTF-8 and contain non-ASCII. If they are ASCII-only, keep the current behaviour. Legacy pages almost never use the HTML5 doctype, which limits breakage. 2. **Late correction.** If a document was decoded with the locale fallback, and the first non-ASCII run (within some bound, e.g. the first 64 KiB) is valid UTF-8 and invalid or implausible in the fallback encoding, re-navigate with UTF-8. Gecko already has a similar reload path for the legacy detector. 3. **Potentially trustworthy origins only.** Apply (1) or (2) only to secure contexts, or only to `localhost`, where the content is very unlikely to be legacy. I would like to know whether implementers would be open to measuring (1) or (2), for example with use counters for "unlabeled, HTML5 doctype, valid non-ASCII UTF-8 in the first N KiB".
